Process-related impurity · immunogenicity risk assessment · RUO

HLA-DR immunogenicity of dsRNA_7071_A08

A 132-residue dsRNA affinity-chromatography ligand — a double-stranded-RNA-binding domain fused to a Protein A Z-domain variant — screened across a 25-molecule HLA-DR panel covering 97.3% of the weighted US/EU population, scored against benchmark affinity ligands and assay controls run in the same batch.

The risk is concentrated, not diffuse. One region — residues 35–52, binding core FIVEAKIKE, peak 15-mer HKKKFIVEAKIKEYR — is presented by 9 of the 25 DR molecules and reaches 55% of the weighted US/EU population. That single peptide is what a confirmatory assay should be built around; the rest of the sequence is unremarkable for a non-human protein of this size.

State the headline as a range, not a point. The 1.77× figure depends on the near-self down-weight, which is set by judgement and which the benchmark could not bound (see the tolerance filter). Across the full plausible range of that weight the ligand moves between 1.61× and 2.06× the Protein A benchmark. The conclusion is stable over that interval — the ligand is above the benchmark throughout and never approaches the positive controls — but the second decimal is not a real number, and this ligand is more exposed to the choice than an antibody-derived one would be, because the single core being down-weighted is its dominant epitope.

On the intrinsic scale the ligand sits at 0.80 population-weighted non-self epitope units per 100 residues, against 0.45 for the Protein A Z-domain — a modestly-elevated result on the calibrated scale. Both numbers come from the same batch, the same panel and the same thresholds, which is the only reason the comparison means anything. Read on for what the batch controls say about whether the batch is reportable at all, and for the exposure arithmetic that turns this into a dose-level call.

Which half of the molecule carries the risk?

dsRNA_7071_A08 is not one domain. It is a fusion, and the two halves have entirely different regulatory standing, so scoring it as a single object answers the wrong question. A whole-molecule fold-change over the Protein A benchmark is in part a comparison of this ligand with a piece of itself — which is why the pipeline was extended with a domain attribution step for this run rather than reporting the headline alone.

Is the novel domain actually foreign? Assigned in this run, not taken on assertion. Aligned against 20,431 reviewed human Swiss-Prot proteins, the closest human relatives of residues 1–72 are STAU1_HUMAN (O95793, 30.6% identity over 62 aa), DSRAD_HUMAN (P55265, 41.8% identity over 55 aa). Both are double-stranded-RNA-binding proteins, which corroborates the fold call — and both sit far below any identity at which pre-existing tolerance could be argued. The domain is a dsRBD, and it is not a human one. (Search seeded on shared 5-mers over 101 candidate proteins and ranked on alignment score, not percent identity; a seeded search can miss a remote homologue, so this bounds the nearest hit rather than proving none is closer.)

The scaffold half scores like the benchmark, because it essentially is the benchmark. Per 100 aa the Z-domain half of the ligand carries 0.45 pIRS units against 0.45 for ProteinA_Z scored standalone in the same batch — the same number to two decimals. 4 of its 5 predicted epitopes overlap an epitope the benchmark already carries, so they are not new exposure: they are the epitope content of a leachate that has been administered to patients for decades. The 7 substitutions that distinguish this scaffold from the wild-type domain created 1 epitope the benchmark does not carry, contributing 0.00 to pIRS.

The epitopes the engineering created

FDKEQQAAR7850.8010.0%79, 84, 86

Read that zero carefully. FDKEQQAAR is predicted to be presented, but only by a DRB3/4/5 molecule — and DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5 carry no frequencies in the DRB1-locus tables the coverage model uses, so their population weight is structurally zero. It is not a statement that nobody presents this peptide. DRB5*01:01 in particular travels on the DR15 haplotype and is common in European populations. The honest reading is that this epitope is real, narrow, and unquantifiable on the population scale this report uses; if the scaffold's engineering is revisited, it is the one scaffold position worth looking at.

The panel had to be designed, not inherited

The usual starting point is the HLA-DR subset of the IEDB class II reference set — 15 molecules, widely described as broadly representative. Measured against the IEDB allele-frequency tables it is not: it reaches 90.1% US-Caucasian and 85.8% European DRB1 phenotypic coverage, 84.2% on the weighted US/EU composite. A 95–98% requirement is not met by that set at any size, because the missing coverage sits in alleles it does not contain.

Growing the panel greedily against measured coverage instead reaches the target at 21 DRB1 molecules (97.27% weighted US/EU), plus the four DRB3/4/5 molecules for the second DR molecule most people express — 25 DR molecules in total.

Coverage is single-locus Hardy–Weinberg phenotypic frequency over the IEDB tables, including the tool's renormalisation for populations whose allele frequencies sum above 1 — reproducing calculate_population_coverage.py to two decimals. DRB3/4/5 carry no frequencies in those tables, so they add presentation breadth without entering this arithmetic and are never double-counted. US Asian coverage lands at 85% and US Amerindian at 67%: a US/EU-weighted objective does not buy those populations, and reaching them needs DRB1*04:05, *12:02, *15:02 and *14:54 added explicitly.

The batch carries its own controls

A ligand run on its own produces a number nobody can size. This batch runs it beside two positive controls (tetanus toxin universal T-helper epitope regions, which the panel must find), two human self proteins (which the tolerance filter must suppress), and four benchmark affinity ligands. The batch is reportable only if the controls behave.

How promiscuous is "promiscuous"?

Reporting that a peptide binds 5 of 25 DR molecules invites the question nobody usually answers: compared to what? The batch answers it by carrying three peptides whose promiscuity is an experimental fact rather than a prediction: influenza haemagglutinin HA306-318 and the tetanus toxin epitopes p2 (830–844) and p30 (947–967). Each was checked against IEDB before being used — HA306-318 has positive human DR-restricted T-cell assays on 25 distinct DR molecules, p2 on 6, p30 on 1. PADRE was a candidate and was dropped: IEDB holds no positive human DR-restricted T-cell record for it.

peptideDR molecules at EL %Rank < 1at %Rank < 5best %Rank
influenza HA306-3182/258/250.46
tetanus toxin p26/2515/250.06
tetanus toxin p302/255/250.64
dsRNA_7071_A08 peak epitope (FIVEAKIKE)5/25—0.01

The ligand's dominant core is as promiscuous as the most promiscuous epitope we have evidence for. The three universal epitopes reach 2–6 of 25 DR molecules at EL %Rank < 1; FIVEAKIKE reaches 5/25 — inside that range. It is not an outlier. It is also not innocuous: it sits exactly where a peptide known to drive CD4 responses in most donors sits.

The same table bounds the method's sensitivity. The strong-binder tier recovers only 24% of the DR molecules a universal epitope is actually presented by — HA306-318 is positive in human T-cell assays on 25 distinct DR molecules and clears %Rank < 1 on 2 of the 25 tested here. So a peptide below the tier is unflagged, not cleared, and the confirmatory assays below are scoped on the flagged peptides plus the intact ligand for exactly that reason.

Does the rule actually work?

Everything above this point is a claim about accuracy that had not been tested. The EL+BA consensus rule entered the pipeline on an argument — eluted-ligand scoring over-calls, so make the affinity head agree — and an argument is not evidence. To find out, the rule was scored against ground truth: every HLA-DR-restricted CD4 T-cell assay result IEDB holds for the 25 molecules in this panel, in human hosts.

The consensus rule does not improve discrimination. A paired bootstrap over 9-mer clusters puts the AUC difference between the EL×BA consensus and EL alone at +0.0125, 95% CI [-0.0007, +0.0246]. The interval spans zero — on this evidence the second head adds nothing to ranking, and its value is confined to where the threshold is placed.

The rule now in use sits at 16% sensitivity and 96% specificity. The threshold that maximises Matthews correlation on this benchmark is GEO %Rank < 5.89, at 45% / 79% — MCC 0.259 against 0.188. That trade runs the wrong way for this application: it flags roughly three times as many peptides to gain sensitivity, and the chance any one of them is real falls from 16% to 10%. When the deliverable is a shortlist of peptides to send into a wet-lab assay, precision is what is being bought. The stricter cut stays, and MCC is the wrong objective to have optimised for here.

Stratifying by source removes the obvious confound: the benchmark's positives are 13% human-derived and its negatives 8%, so a predictor that merely recognised "foreign" would score well for the wrong reason. Within the non-self stratum (n = 5225) the best rule reaches AUC 0.675; within the self stratum (n = 570) 0.585. The discrimination is not an artefact of foreignness.

Read the absolute numbers as an upper bound. NetMHCIIpan is trained on IEDB binding-affinity and mass-spec eluted-ligand data. The labels here are T-cell assay outcomes — a different endpoint it was not trained on — but many of these peptides also carry binding measurements in IEDB, so partial training-set overlap is certain and cannot be excluded from outside. The comparison between rules is far more robust: every rule uses the same two possibly-leaky predictors on the same peptides, so leakage inflates them together and largely cancels in the difference. IEDB's negatives also carry their own bias — a peptide tested and found negative in one donor set is not a clean non-binder — which inflates apparent specificity in both directions equally.

Does breadth beat the best single rank?

One obvious lever was left. The pipeline flags a peptide when any one DR molecule ranks it strongly; the standard intuition is that a peptide presented by many molecules is the more credible epitope, so requiring breadth should raise specificity. That is testable. Every one of the 1,200 benchmark peptides (600 positive, one peptide per 9-mer cluster) was scored against all 25 panel molecules, and four breadth metrics were compared against the best single-allele %Rank with a paired cluster bootstrap on the AUC difference.

The lever does not exist. Against the best single-allele rank, breadth at %Rank < 1 is worth +0.0005 AUC, 95% CI [-0.0156, +0.0169], and population-weighted presentation +0.0013 [-0.0197, +0.0221]. Both intervals straddle zero and both are an order of magnitude smaller than the gap that would justify changing the rule. Counting molecules adds nothing that the single best rank does not already carry.

The confound, and the stratum that removes it

The intuition feels right for a reason that has nothing to do with biology. A peptide's measured breadth in a benchmark is bounded by how many molecules anyone bothered to test it on, and peptides get tested repeatedly because they already looked interesting. That alone is a strong classifier here: test count by itself reaches AUC 0.575, higher than every sequence-derived predictor in the table above.

So the comparison that counts is the one inside a single test-count stratum. Among the 1,069 peptides tested on exactly one molecule (490 positive), where measured breadth cannot be inflated by ascertainment, breadth is still flat: +0.0054 [-0.0113, +0.0221] for breadth and +0.0119 [-0.0111, +0.0315] for population-weighted presentation. In the 131 multi-allele peptides — 84% of them positive, so the stratum is small and unbalanced — breadth is significantly worse than the best rank (-0.0877 [-0.1599, -0.0145]). Neither stratum supports the change.

What this changes: nothing, deliberately. Requiring two molecules lifts specificity 0.61 → 0.79, but sensitivity falls 0.47 → 0.28 and Matthews correlation barely moves (0.074 → 0.086) — the gate is buying specificity with sensitivity at roughly par, not adding information. The pipeline already flags per molecule on %Rank and already uses population weighting only to aggregate and report hits, never to decide them. This result says that arrangement is correct and closes off the tempting addition of a “presented by at least N molecules” or “at least 20% of the population” criterion. It is the fourth proposed improvement in this pipeline to be rejected by measurement rather than adopted by argument.

Two heads, and what the second one is worth

Every 15-mer of every sequence was scored on both NetMHCIIpan heads across all 25 DR molecules: eluted-ligand likelihood, which models what gets presented, and binding affinity, which models peptide–MHC stability. Until this run the pipeline required both to agree before calling a strong binder, on the argument that eluted-ligand scoring over-calls.

The argument did not survive measurement. Against the labelled benchmark, the affinity gate removed 23 true positives and 6 false positives — roughly four real epitopes for every false one — and Matthews correlation went from 0.188 without the gate to 0.184 with it. Eluted-ligand scoring does over-call; the affinity head simply does not remove the over-calls selectively. The gate is now off. Affinity is still predicted and reported for every peptide; it no longer vetoes a call.

Eluted-ligand scoring calls 329 strong binders across the batch, and with the gate off all 329 are used. This is not a cosmetic change: it moved the test article from 2.9× the Protein A benchmark to 1.77×, because the gate had been suppressing the benchmark's epitopes harder than the test article's. An unvalidated rule was setting the headline.

Hits a human repertoire has already seen are not risk

A predicted DR binder whose 9-mer core also occurs in the human proteome is a core the repertoire has had the chance to be tolerised against. Counting those alongside genuinely foreign ones inflates every protein that shares structure with something human — antibody-derived ligands worst of all, since their frameworks are near-identical to human germline V. Each core here is compared to every 9-mer of the human Swiss-Prot proteome: 18.2% are exact human 9-mers, 4.1% are one substitution away.

The threshold is validated rather than asserted. Re-running the identical screen on cores drawn from shuffled versions of the same sequences — a null with the same composition and no real self-similarity — gives a hit rate of 1.4% at the 8/9 cut against 22.3% for real cores, an enrichment of 16.53×. A 5-of-9 "TCR-face" screen, the obvious shortcut, was tried first and discarded: with only five positions specified it matches the human proteome by chance several times per query and flags nearly everything.

Why this filter is not optional. Human germline VH3-23 — a sequence every human is tolerised to by construction — scores a peak promiscuity of 6/25 DR molecules on this panel, more than the test article's 5/25, and an unfiltered pIRS of 0.37 against the test article's 0.93. On raw binder counts a sequence nobody can respond to is indistinguishable from one that matters. After the filter the germline control falls to 0.00 and the ranking becomes readable.

For this ligand the filter is a light touch rather than the whole story: it removes 14% of the raw score, all of it from a single core. That is the expected behaviour for a non-antibody scaffold — there is no germline framework here for the filter to strip — and it means this ligand's ranking rests on the prediction rather than on the filter's judgement calls.

The one number in the filter that is still a guess

The near-self weight — how much credit a core one substitution away from human keeps — is set to 0.35 by judgement, not by evidence. The benchmark was asked to bound it, and could not: among predicted binders, self-like peptides are positive at 0.83 against 0.81 for foreign ones — a ratio of 1.02, 95% CI [0.914, 1.123]. That interval is consistent with almost any weight, so it neither supports nor refutes 0.35.

The reason is ascertainment, and it is not fixable from this data: self peptides reach IEDB overwhelmingly because somebody assayed them for autoimmunity or tumour immunology, so the self peptides nobody responds to are missing from the denominator.

Where the filter is wrong, measured

The filter's rule is "self implies tolerated". That is right often enough to be worth applying and wrong often enough to be worth measuring, so the batch carries two controls that sit on the boundary.

controlroleDR at %Rank<1at <5cores called tolerisedpIRS unfilteredpIRS filtered
MBP_85_99self immunogenic control10/2520/253/31.190.00
CLIP_87_101tolerised binder control1/257/251/10.000.00

The filter suppresses a real epitope, and this is the clearest example of it. Myelin basic protein 85–99 is a human self peptide with positive DR-restricted T-cell assays on 10 distinct DR molecules in IEDB. On this panel it is the broadest binder in the whole batch — 10/25 DR molecules at the strong-binder tier, unfiltered pIRS 1.19, higher than any ligand here. The tolerance filter takes it to 0.00. That is the filter working as designed and being wrong: self-derived epitopes exist, autoimmunity is what they are, and a sequence-identity filter cannot see the difference. It is safe for an affinity ligand because a foreign scaffold's framework similarity to human germline is the case the filter was built for — not for anything where self-reactivity is the question.

The opposite control behaves too. CLIP occupies the groove of essentially every DR molecule as the invariant chain's placeholder, yet carries no positive human DR T-cell record in IEDB. Here it reaches 7/25 DR molecules at the weak tier and 1/25 at the strong tier, and ends at pIRS 0.00 — binding strength alone is not being read as risk.

The filter is doing work, not deleting indiscriminately: the two human self controls lose 100% of their unfiltered score, while the test article loses 14%.

The measured endpoint is an antibody, not a T cell

An ADA assay detects antibodies. A B cell only class-switches with help from a CD4 T cell recognising a peptide from the same protein, so the regions worth carrying into wet-lab work first are those where a non-self DR cluster and a predicted B-cell epitope coincide.

Linear B-cell prediction (BepiPred-2.0) is the weakest model in this pipeline — most real ADA epitopes are conformational. This layer prioritises regions; it is never a standalone claim.

Intrinsic risk × dose

A leached ligand is an impurity, and impurity risk is intrinsic potential multiplied by how much a patient receives. At the ligand's 13.5 kDa, the exposure grid across plausible leachate levels and doses is:

Bands are an internal triage convention, not a regulatory threshold. No agency publishes a numeric leachate immunogenicity limit; the ICH Q6B / EMA expectation is control to a justified, consistently achieved level. Replace the grid in config/config.yaml with your product's actual leachate data and dose.

If the ligand can be re-engineered

Every one of the 19 substitutions was placed at each MHC-II anchor pocket (P1, P4, P6, P9) of the dominant core and the mutated 15-mer re-scored across the panel — 76 variants in all. Wild type is presented by 6 DR molecules reaching 30% of the weighted population.

The knockouts and the designable changes are not the same substitutions. 8 variants abolish predicted presentation entirely, but every one of them is chemically disruptive — the best BLOSUM62 score among them is -1, and they sit at buried framework positions where that is a real stability risk. The most conservative useful change is P6_K40E (K->E, BLOSUM62 +1 — cysteine substitutions are excluded as disulfide-scrambling liabilities), which cuts presentation from 30% to 7.2% without a chemically radical substitution. That is the trade-off to take to a stability screen — not a knockout that would probably cost the fold.

This scan uses the eluted-ligand head alone, so wild-type breadth reads 6/25 here against 5/25 on the EL+BA consensus call used everywhere else — the comparison between variants is what carries the meaning, not the absolute breadth. The "% pop" column counts DRB1 molecules only, so a variant can read 0.0% while one or two DRB3/4/5 molecules still bind it. And this models DR presentation only: effect on ligand–target affinity, resin capacity and alkaline stability is not modelled, and any candidate has to go back through binding and stability screens before it means anything.

What this is, and what it is not

In-silico DR screening ranks and localises risk. It does not measure it. pIRS is a relative scale readable only against the benchmarks in this batch; it is not a predicted ADA incidence, and no in-silico method available today predicts one. The specific limits that matter for how far this output can be pushed:

  • Prediction, not presentation. NetMHCIIpan scores peptide–MHC binding. It does not model antigen uptake, endosomal proteolysis, HLA-DM editing or the ligand's conformational stability in the endosome — all of which decide what is actually presented.
  • DR only. DP and DQ contribute to CD4 responses and are excluded here by the sponsor's panel specification. DQ in particular is implicated in several biologic ADA responses.
  • The tolerance filter is a screen, not JanusMatrix. It does not require the human counterpart peptide to bind the same allele, so it errs toward calling more peptides tolerised. Every flagged core is written out with the human protein it matched, so each call is checkable.
  • No aggregation, no adjuvant effect, no repeat-dose modelling. Aggregated or particulate impurity is substantially more immunogenic than the monomer, and none of that is in scope for a sequence-based method.
  • The benchmark anchor is an argument, not a measurement. Protein A Z-domain leachate has a long controlled clinical history, but "comparable predicted epitope content to Protein A" is an inference about risk, not evidence of it.

Recommended confirmatory work (all available RUO)

  1. HLA-DR competitive binding on the 8 flagged peptides against the panel's dominant molecules — directly confirms the predicted binding, days not months, lowest cost.
  2. MAPPs (MHC-associated peptide proteomics) on monocyte-derived dendritic cells from HLA-typed donors — shows what is actually processed and presented from the intact ligand, which no predictor can.
  3. Ex-vivo PBMC / CD4 T-cell proliferation across ~50 HLA-typed donors matched to this panel, using the flagged peptides plus whole ligand — the closest available surrogate for clinical ADA risk.

All three are scoped by the peptide list this pipeline produces, which is the practical point of running it: it turns "assess the ligand" into a defined, costed experiment on 8 peptides.

Inputs and provenance

The test article dsRNA_7071_A08 is sponsor-supplied and proprietary — it has no public database identifier, and none is required: the pipeline works from de-identified FASTA alone. Every other sequence in the batch is public and was fetched live from RCSB or UniProt with the accession shown below, so the comparators and controls are reproducible even though the test article is not. The hallmark tetrad is FR2 Kabat 37/44/45/47: camelid VHHs carry F/Y–E–R–G/L where a human VH carries V–G–L–W. It separates a humanised VHH from a native camelid one at a glance, and that distinction is a better predictor of clinical ADA than epitope count alone.
